title: Key-frame strip of an animation: what happens over time, at a glance?
summary: When a result is an animation, a strip of key frames with time stamps shows what happens at a glance, on paper or in a report. Four frames of a moving blob illustrate the form.

media.alt: A strip of four square colour images titled t = 0.0 s, 0.5 s, 1.0 s and 1.5 s, each showing a bright round blob on a dark purple background that moves from the right edge to the left edge.
media.caption: Reference render of class F6.4 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: What happens over time, at a glance?
read_the_figure.axes: Four panels in a row, sharing a vertical axis, with the same fixed spatial window in each (here minus 1 to 1 in x and y, with the tick labels removed). The panel titles are the time stamps.
look_at: What changes from frame to frame (position, size, brightness)? What stays fixed?
Is the colour map the same in every frame and is there a scale (here there is not)?
Is the spacing in time even, and is it fine enough to follow the features?
Could you tell from the strip how fast the feature moves, in the units of the axes?
as_drawn: Four frames at t = 0.0, 0.5, 1.0 and 1.5 s. A Gaussian blob of full width at half maximum about 0.58 moves from x of about +0.6 to about -0.6 (centre shifts -0.4 per frame).
Same size and brightness in every frame, so the motion is a pure translation, at about -0.8 length units per second.
The viridis colour map is the same in all frames, but there is no colour bar and the tick labels are removed, so neither the values nor the length unit can be read.
The time stamps are above each frame in seconds, which is the class's required item.
read_the_figure.proves: A key-frame strip proves what the sampled frames show: that at those four instants the blob is where it is. It cannot show what happens between the frames and gives only a coarse estimate of speed.
if_wrong: No time stamps: the reader cannot order the frames or read a speed.
Colour scales that differ between frames: brightness changes then mean nothing.
Frame spacing larger than the feature: the reader cannot tell which blob in one frame became which in the next.
must_check: time stamps: without them the strip is a set of unlabelled pictures, and no rate can be read from it.

terms.meaning: One selected frame of an animation, chosen to show a stage of the process.
The time value printed with a frame, with its unit.
The same axes limits and colour limits in every frame, so that changes are changes in the data.
The width of a bump where it falls to half of its peak: for a Gaussian, 2.355 times the standard deviation.
A change of position without any change of shape.

remember: Use the same axes and the same colour scale in every frame.
Print the time with its unit on each frame.
Frame spacing should be smaller than the feature size divided by its speed.
Add a colour bar and a length scale.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Each panel is a colour image of a field on a fixed window; brightness encodes the field's value through a single colour map (dark purple low, yellow high). Panels are in time order from left to right, and the title of each is its time stamp. Panels share the vertical axis so the position of the blob can be compared across frames.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: Plain language: an animation cannot be printed, but a few well-chosen stills can tell the same story. Putting them in a row, in time order, with the same axes, lets your eye follow the blob from frame to frame. The time stamps turn pictures into a measurement: distance moved divided by time elapsed is the speed.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: Between the frames anything can happen: a strip hides fast events. If the frames are too far apart the viewer may link the wrong blobs or see motion in the wrong direction (temporal aliasing). Without a colour bar or length scale the picture is qualitative. Frames chosen at uneven times, or with a different colour scale each, create false changes.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: A space-time diagram (position against time, brightness as colour) shows the whole history in one picture. A line plot of a tracked quantity such as the blob centre against time gives speed directly. A short video or interactive slider is better when the reader needs every detail.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Add a shared colour bar and a length scale bar, mark the blob centre in each frame with a cross, and draw the centre's path as a dotted line over all frames, with the speed written beneath.

steps.title: Width of the blob
steps.note: This is the width of the bump in the render, in axis units; verified numerically.

steps.title: Speed from two frames
steps.note: The centre moves 0.4 units in each 0.5 s interval, towards negative x.

steps.title: Is the frame rate enough?
steps.note: The shift between frames is smaller than the blob's width, so consecutive blobs overlap and can be matched by eye.

worked.title: Reading the motion from the reference render
worked.problem: (1) What is the speed and direction of the blob? (2) Is the frame spacing fine enough to follow it? (3) When would the blob's centre reach the left edge of the window if the motion continued?

solution.text: (1) The centre goes from about +0.6 in the first frame to about -0.6 in the fourth frame in 1.5 s.
(2) The shift per frame is 0.4 and the blob is 0.58 wide at half maximum, so successive blobs overlap.
(3) The centre must travel from 0.6 to -1.

worked.answer: Speed 0.8 units per second towards negative x; yes, the 0.4 shift per frame is below the 0.58 width; the centre reaches the left edge at 2.0 s.

analyze.q: Why does the picture not tell you the speed in metres per second, even though it has time stamps?
If the frames were 2 s apart, what could go wrong with your reading?
How would you check that the colour scale is the same in every frame?

evaluate.q: A reviewer wants the strip replaced by a movie. When is the strip enough and when is it not?

create: Add a colour bar, a scale bar and a dotted path of the centre to the strip.
Make a six-frame strip with logarithmically spaced times for a diffusing blob.

checks.q: Why must the colour scale be the same in every frame?
checks.hint: What does a colour change mean?
checks.answer: A colour change should mean a change in the data; with different scales per frame the same value gets different colours and false changes appear.

checks.q: A blob moves 0.3 units between frames 0.2 s apart. What is its speed?
Frame spacing is much larger than the blob's width. What goes wrong?
checks.answer: You cannot tell which blob in one frame became which in the next (or even the direction); the motion is under-sampled in time, like aliasing in sampled signals.
